page.title: Integrating Golfer and Golf Club Detection Models
page.description: Adapting a unified golfer-and-club training pipeline to incomplete annotations, improving club recall under heavy motion blur.
page.eyebrow: Computer vision · Learning from incomplete annotations
page.role: My role: I redesigned the data pipeline and annotation-aware training loss, integrated two annotation sources, and trained the unified keypoint model.
page.footer: Integrating Golfer and Golf Club Detection Models

banner.label: Unified golfer and golf club detection

sections.title: Abstract
paragraphs: To replace a fragile two-model pipeline, I revised data preparation and the training loss to learn a unified golfer-and-club keypoint model from incomplete annotations. Combining two models into one approximately doubled overall inference speed and improved club recall by around 50% on heavily blurred cases, demonstrating the value of annotation-aware training without full relabeling.

metrics.label: Club recall improvement on heavily blurred cases

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: The legacy system used separate bounding-box models for golfer pose and golf club detection, then reconstructed a connected skeleton through post-processing. Recovering club orientation required choosing between bounding-box diagonals using pose estimates, which was unreliable when the club was nearly vertical.

A unified keypoint model could predict body and club geometry directly, but the available datasets did not consistently label both targets in the same frames. Missing annotations reflected gaps in labeling, not necessarily missing objects. The previous training setup treated these gaps as negative examples and suppressed valid predictions.
The research question was whether an annotation-aware data and training pipeline could combine these incomplete sources and improve club recall without requiring a fully relabeled dataset.

sections.title: Methods

subsections.title: Represent annotation availability
items: Issue: Golfer and club labels came from different sources and covered different frames. A missing label could not reliably be interpreted as object absence.

Approach: I redesigned the data pipeline to merge the sources while retaining which targets were annotated in each training sample. This preserved usable supervision without assigning negative meaning to unavailable labels.

subsections.title: Align the loss with incomplete supervision
items: Issue: The existing training structure penalized predictions for unlabeled targets, contradicting the dataset’s annotation coverage.

Approach: I revised the loss and training structure to account for annotation availability, so missing labels did not incorrectly suppress valid detections. The central change was how supervision was interpreted, rather than requiring every frame to be fully annotated.

subsections.title: Predict body and club keypoints together
items: Issue: Separate bounding-box outputs required orientation inference and output alignment before they could form one skeleton.

Approach: I retained the backbone architecture shared by the legacy models and replaced the detection outputs with a lightweight keypoint head. One model learned golfer pose and club geometry together, giving club estimation access to body-pose context.

sections.note: Proprietary loss formulations, training settings, and internal data-processing details are omitted.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: The unified model improved club recall by approximately 50% on heavily motion-blurred cases, where body-pose context supported estimates despite weak club visibility. It also ran at roughly the speed of one legacy model, approximately doubling overall inference speed relative to the two-model pipeline.
sections.note: The selected examples illustrate observed behavior. They are not a controlled benchmark, and the reported recall improvement is specific to the difficult cases assessed.

subsections.title: Supervision must reflect what is actually labeled
paragraphs: The main contribution was making the training pipeline compatible with incomplete annotations. Treating every unlabeled target as absent introduced conflicting supervision; accounting for annotation availability allowed the two sources to contribute to one model.

Compared with the earlier two-model system, joint prediction also removed the bounding-box-to-skeleton conversion. The blurred-club examples suggest that body-pose context can help when direct club evidence is weak.

subsections.title: Implications for CI/CD and MLOps
paragraphs: A unified keypoint output reduces the model interfaces and concurrent output-alignment logic that must be maintained and tested. The simpler conversion, deployment, and verification workflow saved approximately 2–3 days of engineering work per model upgrade.

From an MLOps perspective, annotation availability and joint definitions become explicit data contracts. Future CI/CD checks can validate those contracts and track club recall on held-out difficult examples before accepting a model update.

subsections.title: Limitations
paragraphs: The selected snapshots and videos do not establish generalization across all golfers, camera views, or recording conditions. Interpreting the reported recall improvement requires the evaluation set, matching criteria, and baseline definition; those details are not presented here.
The examples also do not isolate the effect of the revised loss from joint body–club learning. Controlled ablations and held-out evaluation would be needed to measure their separate contributions.

subsections.title: Future directions
paragraphs: The pipeline can accommodate future company pose formats by mapping joint definitions and tracking unavailable labels. This supports changes in skeleton format without requiring all historical annotations to be made identical.

The same principle could support reuse of existing annotations from datasets such as COCO and Human3.6M. That extension would require validating joint semantics, coordinate conventions, and domain differences; it is a potential application rather than a demonstrated result of this project.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: Revising the data pipeline and loss made incomplete annotations usable for a unified keypoint model and improved club recall. The result supports annotation-aware supervision as a practical foundation for future dataset and skeleton changes.
